brief.topic: A Little Agreement at Every Edge

s01: Follow one line through these tiles.
It bends, meets a neighbor, and keeps going.
A whole pattern grows from one small choice.
Lift a single tile from the middle.
Two curved strokes touch the middle of all four edges.
Turn the tile a quarter turn.
The curves change partners, but those four meeting places stay fixed.
Put the tile back and look closely at one join.
A curve arrives from one tile.
Exactly one curve carries it onward through the next.
There is no loose end here, and no fork to choose.
It can return to its beginning and form a loop.
Or it can reach the outside edge.
On a finite board like this, those are the two possibilities.
Turn a different tile and the routes can change.
The same midpoint rule still joins every neighbor.
This is a Truchet tile pattern.
A little agreement at each edge holds the whole drawing together.

creative.audience: Curious teens and adults; no specialist prerequisites.
creative.learning_goal: A midpoint pairing gives degree two at every interior join; finite components are loops or boundary-to-boundary paths.
creative.question: Why do these tile paths never end inside the pattern?
creative.payoff: A midpoint pairing gives degree two at every interior join; finite components are loops or boundary-to-boundary paths.
creative.transfer_prompt: Notice the changed condition near the end; exploration is optional.
creative.duration_rationale: Measured narration and visible operation determine duration; no fixed length padding.
creative.novelty_audit: Compared archive titles and authored mechanism index before production. Closest prior: Penrose tiling; moire; seven bridges. Difference: Local degree-two connectivity of disjoint quarter arcs, not aperiodicity, beat bands or Euler route existence.. Earlier unavailable transcripts are not fully audited.

profile_application.signature: An original whole pattern, an identified local rule, and a return to the same image with a visible global consequence.
profile_application.episode_variation: Follow an actual connected path, lift and turn its local tile, enlarge a seam, then distinguish a loop from an outer-edge route.
exceptions: Ideal geometry, not a material simulation.
No music bed; eventual audio review scope explicitly recorded.

scenes.narration:
Follow one line through these tiles. It bends, meets a neighbor, and keeps going. A whole pattern grows from one small choice.

Lift a single tile from the middle. Two curved strokes touch the middle of all four edges. Turn the tile a quarter turn. The curves change partners, but those four meeting places stay fixed.

Put the tile back and look closely at one join. A curve arrives from one tile. Exactly one curve carries it onward through the next. There is no loose end here, and no fork to choose.

Now follow a complete path. It can return to its beginning and form a loop. Or it can reach the outside edge. On a finite board like this, those are the two possibilities.

Turn a different tile and the routes can change. The same midpoint rule still joins every neighbor. This is a Truchet tile pattern. A little agreement at each edge holds the whole drawing together.
